slides.title: Why Use Comments
slides.content: Comments explain code intent to other developers and to your future self. The compiler ignores them entirely.
slides.example:
// This calculates the total
int total = price + tax;

exercise.prompt: What happens to comments when the code is compiled?
options: They are ignored by the compiler
They are converted to debug symbols
exercise.answer: They are ignored by the compiler

slides.title: Single-Line Comments
slides.content: Single-line comments start with // and continue to the end of the line. They are the most common comment style.
slides.example:
// Initialize counter
int counter = 0; // starting value

exercise.prompt: Complete a single-line comment: _____ This is a comment

slides.title: Multi-Line Comments
slides.content: Multi-line comments use /* to open and */ to close. They can span multiple lines and cannot be nested.

exercise.prompt: Drag the closing delimiter for a multi-line comment: /* comment text [?]

slides.title: XML Documentation Comments
slides.content: XML doc comments start with /// and support tags like <summary> and <param> for generating documentation.

exercise.prompt: Write an XML doc comment opening for a method that gets a user name.
exercise.expectedOutput: The compiler ignores the comment and compiles normally.
hints: Make sure your code includes the required keywords/elements: ///
When run, your code should output: The compiler ignores the comment and compiles normally.

slides.title: Commenting Out Code
slides.content: Developers use comments to temporarily disable code during debugging or testing.

exercise.prompt: Why might you comment out a line of code?

slides.title: Best Practices
slides.content: Write comments for why, not what. The code already shows what it does; comments should clarify intent and rationale.
slides.example:
// Use binary search because the list is sorted
int index = BinarySearch(items, target);

exercise.prompt: Good comments explain the _____ rather than restating the code.

slides.title: Avoiding Bad Comments
slides.content: Obvious comments add noise. Redundant comments become outdated and misleading. Prefer clear code over explanatory comments.

exercise.prompt: Drag the better comment for this code: counter++; [?] counter++;

slides.title: Comments Review
slides.content: Use // for single lines, /* */ for blocks, and /// for XML docs. Keep comments meaningful and up to date.

exercise.prompt: Write a single-line comment followed by a Console.WriteLine statement.
hints: Make sure your code includes the required keywords/elements: //
When run, your code should output: Hello!

slides.title: Flow Builder: Comment and Output
slides.content: Drag a Comment block then an Output block to show how comments sit beside executable code.

exercise.prompt: Build a flow with a comment 'Hello' then output 'World!'
